prompt: Which driving ability is usually the first to be affected when a person drinks alcohol?
choices: Coordination
Muscle strength
Hearing
Judgment
explanation: Judgment is the first ability alcohol affects, which is why drinkers often decide they are fine to drive. Vision, reaction time and coordination are impaired as more alcohol builds up.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 22, FL p. 43, TX p. 61)

prompt: What is the only thing that lowers your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) after drinking?
choices: Drinking black coffee
Time
Taking a cold shower
Eating a large meal
explanation: Only time sobers you up, because your body removes alcohol at a slow, steady rate. Coffee, cold showers and food do not lower your BAC.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 62, PA p. 38, NJ p. 116)

prompt: What type of drug is alcohol?
choices: A stimulant that speeds up your reactions
Not a drug at all, just a beverage
A depressant that slows down the brain and body
A painkiller that only affects muscles
explanation: Alcohol is a depressant drug. It slows reflexes, reduces alertness and interferes with judgment and vision, even though some drinkers feel more energetic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 22, TX p. 61, NJ p. 116)

prompt: Which of these contains about the same amount of alcohol as a 12-ounce can of regular beer?
choices: Half of a 1.5-ounce shot of liquor
A 12-ounce glass of wine
A glass holding 4 ounces of 80-proof liquor
A 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor
explanation: A 12-ounce regular beer, a standard glass of wine and a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor each hold about the same amount of alcohol. A 12-ounce glass of wine or 4 ounces of liquor is several standard drinks.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 55, NJ p. 117, PA p. 38, CA p. 79)

prompt: Your friend says beer is a "safer" choice than liquor if you plan to drive later. What is true?
choices: Beer is safer, so you can drink more of it before driving
Wine affects driving less than beer or liquor does
No drink is safer; what matters is how much alcohol you have
Only liquor can raise your BAC enough to affect driving
explanation: The type of drink makes no difference. A regular beer, a glass of wine and a shot of liquor have about the same alcohol, so what counts is how much you drink. None is safe before driving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 22, AL p. 35, NY p. 55)

prompt: Which of these helps determine your blood alcohol concentration (BAC)?
choices: Whether you drank beer or liquor, no matter how much
How many years of driving experience you have
How many drinks you had and how quickly you drank them
Whether you feel drunk
explanation: BAC depends on how much alcohol you drink, how fast you drink it, your body weight and whether you have eaten. Driving experience and how you feel do not change it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 117, NY p. 55, TX p. 62)

prompt: Two friends drink the same amount of alcohol over the same period of time. One weighs 120 pounds and the other weighs 200 pounds. Who will most likely have the higher BAC?
choices: The 200-pound friend
They will have exactly the same BAC
It depends only on which type of drink they had
The 120-pound friend
explanation: Body weight affects BAC: the same amount of alcohol is more concentrated in a smaller person. That is why one drink can affect a lighter person more.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 38, NJ p. 117, CA p. 79)

prompt: How does eating food before or while drinking affect your BAC?
choices: It slows absorption but cannot prevent impairment
It makes you sober by soaking up the alcohol
It lets you safely drink twice as much before driving
It has no effect on how alcohol is absorbed
explanation: Food slows how fast alcohol enters your bloodstream, but heavy drinking still produces a high BAC. Eating does not make a person sober.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 117, NY p. 56)

prompt: After several drinks, your friend says two cups of strong coffee will make him sober enough to drive. Is he right?
choices: Yes. Each cup of coffee cancels out about one drink
Yes, as long as he also drinks a glass of cold water
Only if he waits ten minutes after drinking the coffee
No. Coffee may make him more alert, but his BAC stays the same
explanation: Caffeine can make a drinker feel more alert, but it cannot change BAC or make a drunk driver sober. Only time removes alcohol from the body.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 61, NY p. 56, PA p. 38)

prompt: On average, about how long does it take the body to get rid of the alcohol in one standard drink?
choices: About one hour
About 10 minutes
About 4 hours
It leaves as soon as you stop drinking
explanation: On average the body removes about one standard drink per hour, and some people take longer. Four drinks take about four hours to wear off, not minutes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 62, NY p. 55, AK p. 22, PA p. 38)

prompt: You had four drinks at a party that just ended. You ate a big meal and had a coffee, and you feel fine. What should you do?
choices: Do not drive; get a sober ride or stay the night
Drive home slowly using quiet back roads
Wait 15 minutes for the coffee to work, then drive
Drink some water and drive with the windows open
explanation: Food and coffee do not lower your BAC, and feeling fine is not a reliable sign because alcohol affects judgment first. Several drinks take several hours to leave your body, so the only safe choice is not to drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 62, NJ p. 117, FL p. 43)

prompt: Which organ removes most of the alcohol from your body?
choices: The stomach
The lungs
The liver
The skin, through sweat
explanation: Most alcohol is broken down by the liver at a steady rate; only a small amount leaves through breath, urine and sweat. That is why exercise or "sweating it out" does not sober you up.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 116, AK p. 22)

prompt: Which of these over-the-counter medicines is most likely to make you drowsy and affect your driving?
choices: Cold or allergy medicine
Antacid tablets for heartburn
A daily multivitamin
Saline nasal spray
explanation: Many cold and allergy medicines (such as antihistamines) can cause drowsiness. Read the label for warnings before you drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 44, PA p. 38, TX p. 61, NJ p. 119)

prompt: Is it legal to drive while impaired by a medicine your doctor prescribed for you?
choices: No. Impaired driving is illegal even with a valid prescription
Yes. A valid prescription is a legal defense
Yes, as long as you carry the labeled pill bottle with you
Yes. Impaired-driving laws only cover alcohol and illegal drugs
explanation: Impaired-driving laws apply to any drug that affects your ability to drive, whether it is illegal, prescribed or bought over the counter. Having a prescription does not make impaired driving legal.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 78, FL p. 44, NJ p. 119, NY p. 54)

prompt: The label on your medicine says "May cause drowsiness. Do not operate heavy machinery." What does this mean for you?
choices: Do not drive after taking it; a car counts as heavy machinery
Nothing; the warning is only for people who run construction equipment
You may still drive, as long as the trip is short
You may drive if you take it with coffee to stay alert
explanation: A warning about heavy machinery includes your car. If a medicine may make you drowsy, do not drive after taking it, and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 38, NJ p. 119)

prompt: You are not sure whether a new medicine will affect your driving. What should you do?
choices: Take it and see how you feel while driving
Drive only during daylight hours
Ask your doctor or pharmacist before driving
Ask a friend who took the same medicine once
explanation: If you are unsure about a medicine's side effects, read the label and check with a doctor or pharmacist before you drive. Testing it out behind the wheel puts everyone at risk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 44, PA p. 38, TX p. 61)

prompt: What happens when alcohol is combined with other drugs or medicines?
choices: The two cancel each other out, so you feel normal
The medicine lowers your BAC and weakens the alcohol
Nothing changes as long as the medicine was prescribed to you
The effects can multiply and be much stronger than either alone
explanation: Mixing alcohol with other drugs often multiplies their effects and can cause serious health problems. Never drink alcohol while taking other drugs without checking with a doctor.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 44, NJ p. 119, NY p. 54, CO p. 8)

prompt: You took an allergy pill this morning. At dinner you have one beer and plan to drive home. What is true?
choices: The beer could affect you like several drinks
One beer is too little to matter, so it is fine to drive
The allergy pill will cancel out the effect of the beer
The effect will be the same as one beer without medicine
explanation: Mixing alcohol and drugs multiplies their effects. One drink combined with an allergy or cold medicine can have the same effect as several drinks, so you should not drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 44, TX p. 61)

prompt: Can marijuana impair your ability to drive?
choices: No. It makes drivers slower and more careful, so it is safer
Yes. It can slow your reactions and affect judgment and coordination
Only when it is used together with alcohol
Not if it is legal to use in the state where you live
explanation: Marijuana impairs reaction time, judgment, coordination and attention, so it is unsafe to drive after using it. Being legal to use does not make it safe or legal to drive impaired.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 38, TX p. 61, NJ p. 119, CO p. 8)

prompt: Adults may legally use marijuana where you live. You used some an hour ago. May you drive?
choices: No. Driving while high is illegal even where marijuana is legal
Yes. A legal product cannot lead to an impaired-driving charge
Yes, as long as you have a medical marijuana card with you
Yes, because smoked marijuana wears off within an hour
explanation: Impaired-driving laws cover any drug that affects your driving, including marijuana that is legal to buy or medically recommended. Do not use marijuana before driving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 54, NY p. 59, MT p. 83, CO p. 8)

prompt: Which driving skills does marijuana commonly affect?
choices: Only your sense of smell and taste
Keeping the car in its lane and judging distances
Only your long-term memory, not driving skills
It sharpens your reaction time and focus
explanation: Marijuana can reduce tracking (the ability to stay in your lane) and distance judgment, and it slows reactions. These are skills you need every second you drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 119, PA p. 38)

prompt: What is a designated driver?
choices: The person in the group who drank the least
Whoever feels the most sober at the end of the night
The person who owns the car, as long as they had only one drink
A person who drinks no alcohol so they can drive others home
explanation: A designated driver stays completely sober and is responsible for getting others home safely. "Drank the least" or "feels fine" is not the same as sober.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 119, NY p. 59, FL p. 43)

prompt: You agreed to be the designated driver tonight. Your friends offer you "just one beer." What should you do?
choices: Have one beer as long as you wait an hour
Say no and drink no alcohol at all
Have one beer if you eat with it
Have a light beer, since it does not count
explanation: A designated driver should not drink any alcohol. Even one drink can affect your driving, so as the sober driver, one drink is one too many.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 43, NY p. 59)

prompt: You have been drinking at a friend's house. Which is a safe way to get home?
choices: Drive home slowly with your hazard lights on
Drive with the windows down so the cold air keeps you alert
Take a taxi, rideshare or transit, or ride with a sober driver
Let the friend who had fewer drinks than you drive
explanation: After drinking, get a ride from someone who has not been drinking, use a taxi or rideshare, take public transit, or stay the night. Fresh air does not sober you up, and a friend who drank less is still impaired.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 43, NJ p. 117, NY p. 59, AK p. 19)

prompt: A friend has been drinking and insists on driving home. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Follow them home to make sure they arrive
Let them drive if they can walk in a straight line
Take their keys and help them get a safe ride home
Give them coffee and then let them drive
explanation: Friends don't let friends drive impaired. Taking the keys and arranging a sober ride, a taxi or a place to sleep prevents a crash; coffee and walking tests do not make someone sober.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 43, NJ p. 118, AZ p. 58)

prompt: You are hosting a party where alcohol is served. Which step helps keep guests from driving impaired?
choices: Serve strong coffee at the end so guests sober up before leaving
Offer alcohol-free drinks and food, and stop serving alcohol early
Keep guests' glasses topped off so no one has to ask for refills
Let guests decide for themselves whether they are fine to drive
explanation: Good hosts offer non-alcoholic drinks and food, never push refills, and stop serving alcohol well before the party ends. If a guest has had too much, do not let them drive. Coffee does not sober anyone up.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 118)

prompt: What does the "implied consent" law mean?
choices: You must sign a consent form before an officer can test you
Officers need your spoken permission before any alcohol test
You agree to let officers search your car at any time
By driving, you have agreed to a chemical test if lawfully asked
explanation: Under implied consent (some states call it express consent), driving in the state means you have already agreed to a breath, blood or urine test when an officer lawfully requests one for suspected impaired driving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 56, CA p. 80, CO p. 8, AK p. 18)

prompt: You are lawfully arrested for impaired driving and refuse the chemical test. What is true?
choices: Nothing happens, because the officer now has no evidence
You can no longer be charged, since there is no test result
Refusing can cost you your license, apart from any DUI charge
The officer must release you and let you drive home
explanation: Refusing a test you agreed to under implied consent carries its own penalties, such as license suspension or revocation. You can still be charged with impaired driving based on other evidence.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 56, TX p. 64, CA p. 80, AK p. 18)

prompt: What does a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) test measure?
choices: How many drinks you had in the past week
How quickly you can react
How much alcohol your liver can store
The amount of alcohol in your blood
explanation: BAC is the percentage of alcohol in your bloodstream. It is usually measured by a breath, blood or urine test.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 55, CA p. 79, NJ p. 117)

prompt: A breath test shows your BAC is below the legal limit, but you were weaving between lanes. Can you still be arrested for impaired driving?
choices: Yes. You can be arrested for impaired driving below the limit
No. Being under the limit means you are legally sober to drive
Only if you also refuse to take a chemical test
Only if your weaving caused a crash or an injury
explanation: Being under the legal limit does not mean it is safe or legal to drive impaired. An officer's observations of your driving and behavior can be enough evidence for an impaired-driving charge.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 79, PA p. 85, TX p. 64)

prompt: Why is a driver who has been drinking often unaware of being impaired?
choices: Alcohol sharpens your senses for the first hour or so
Impairment only starts once you begin to feel drunk
Alcohol does not affect people who say they feel fine
Alcohol makes you feel confident while it weakens your judgment
explanation: Alcohol weakens the skills you need to drive while making you feel more confident. Because judgment is affected first, drinkers are poor judges of whether they are fit to drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 54, PA p. 37, AK p. 23)

prompt: Why is drinking and driving especially dangerous at night?
choices: Your body absorbs alcohol faster after the sun goes down
Night vision is already limited, and alcohol slows glare recovery
Night driving makes alcohol wear off more slowly
Roads are emptier, so drinkers tend to fall asleep sooner
explanation: Night vision is naturally limited, and alcohol further reduces your ability to see clearly and to recover from the glare of oncoming headlights. You can be blinded for a long time.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 54)

prompt: Which behavior may be a sign that another driver is impaired?
choices: Signaling well before turning
Keeping a steady speed with traffic
Weaving or drifting within or across lanes
Stopping smoothly at a red light
explanation: Weaving, jerky speed changes, sudden stops and driving much slower or faster than traffic are common signs of an impaired driver.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 118)

prompt: Which statement about the driving behavior of impaired drivers is true?
choices: They always drive faster than other traffic
They may drive unusually slowly, not only too fast
They always stay perfectly centered in their lane
They are easy to spot because they use their hazard lights
explanation: Impaired drivers may speed, but some drive overly cautiously and much slower than traffic. Other signs include weaving, jerky speed changes and sudden stops at signs or lights.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 118)

prompt: The car ahead of you is weaving across the lane line and braking for no reason. What should you do?
choices: Stay well back, then report it to police when it is safe
Pass it quickly and honk to warn the driver as you go by
Follow closely so you can read the license plate
Pull alongside and signal the driver to pull over
explanation: Stay a safe distance from a suspected impaired driver. Have a passenger call, or pull over safely and call police with the vehicle's description, location and direction of travel. Never try to stop the driver yourself.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 82, NE p. 88, NJ p. 118)

prompt: Compared with older, experienced drivers, young drivers who have been drinking tend to crash:
choices: Only at higher blood alcohol levels
At the same blood alcohol levels
Less often, because their bodies process alcohol faster
At lower blood alcohol levels
explanation: Crashes involving young drinking drivers happen at lower average BAC levels than crashes involving middle-aged or older drivers. Inexperience plus alcohol is especially dangerous.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 22)

prompt: A man and a woman of the same weight drink the same amount in the same period of time. What is most likely?
choices: The man will have a higher BAC
The woman will have a higher BAC
Their BAC will always be exactly the same
Eating first means alcohol will not affect either one
explanation: Because of differences in how bodies process alcohol, a woman drinking the same amount as a man of the same weight may reach a higher BAC and take longer to remove the alcohol.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 38, NY p. 55)

prompt: After surgery, your doctor prescribes an opioid pain medicine. What should you know about driving?
choices: Prescribed medicine is always safe for driving if taken as directed
Relieving your pain will make you a more focused driver
It only matters if you take more than the prescribed dose
It can make you drowsy and slow your reactions, even at the normal dose
explanation: Opioids and many other prescription drugs can cause drowsiness and slow reaction time even at the correct dose. Read the label and ask your doctor or pharmacist before driving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 38, CA p. 78, FL p. 44)

prompt: Two people each have three drinks. One drinks them in one hour; the other spreads them over three hours. Who will likely have the higher BAC?
choices: The person who drank over three hours
Their BAC levels will be the same
The person who drank them in one hour
It depends only on whether the drinks were beer or wine
explanation: BAC depends on how much you drink and how fast. Your body removes alcohol slowly, so drinking quickly builds up a higher BAC.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 117, NY p. 55, PA p. 38)

prompt: How does alcohol affect your reaction time?
choices: It speeds it up
It has no effect until you are legally drunk
It slows it down
It speeds it up after one drink, then slows it
explanation: Alcohol slows your reflexes and reaction time, so you need longer to respond to hazards. It also reduces your ability to judge speed and distance.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 43, NY p. 54, AK p. 22)

prompt: When do the effects of alcohol on your driving begin?
choices: With the first drink, well before the legal limit
Only once your BAC reaches the legal limit
Only after about three drinks for most adults
Only once you start to look or feel drunk
explanation: Alcohol begins to weaken your driving skills with the first drink, even if you do not look or feel drunk. Even one drink raises your crash risk, and experience or tolerance does not protect you. The legal limit is not a safe level.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 54, NY p. 56, PA p. 37, AL p. 35)

prompt: If an officer requests a chemical test under implied consent, what can the test look for?
choices: Alcohol only
Illegal drugs only
Only drugs you have no prescription for
Alcohol and other drugs
explanation: Chemical tests of breath, blood or urine can measure alcohol and can also detect other drugs, including medicines. Impaired-driving laws cover both alcohol and drugs.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 64, CA p. 80, CO p. 8)

prompt: When is the best time to plan how you will get home from an event where you will be drinking?
choices: After your first drink
Before you start drinking
When you are ready to leave
Only if you start to feel drunk
explanation: Plan your ride, such as a designated driver, rideshare or staying over, before you drink. Once you are impaired, your judgment is weaker and you are less likely to make a safe choice.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 59, FL p. 43)

prompt: You drank heavily until 2 a.m. and then slept for four hours. When you wake up at 6 a.m., what is true?
choices: Sleep always clears alcohol from your body
You may still have alcohol in your blood and be impaired
You are sober because you feel rested
A shower and breakfast will make you safe to drive
explanation: Your body removes only about one drink per hour, and sleep does not speed it up. After heavy drinking you can still be impaired the next morning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 62, AK p. 22, PA p. 38)

prompt: Which is true about cough syrup and driving?
choices: Cough syrup cannot affect driving because it is sold without a prescription
Some cough syrups contain alcohol or ingredients that can impair your driving
Cough syrup makes you more alert behind the wheel
Cough syrup only matters if you also drink beer
explanation: Some cough medicines contain alcohol, and many cause drowsiness. Over-the-counter products can impair your driving just like prescription drugs, so read the label first.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 78, PA p. 38)

prompt: After a few drinks, your friend plans to exercise to "sweat out" the alcohol before driving. Will that work?
choices: No. Sweat removes very little alcohol; only time sobers you up
Yes. Hard exercise burns off alcohol much faster than resting
Yes, if he exercises for at least 15 minutes
Yes, if he follows it with a cold shower and coffee
explanation: Exercise, coffee and cold showers cannot reduce BAC. Most alcohol is broken down by the liver at a steady rate, so only time will sober you up.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 56, TX p. 62, NJ p. 116)

prompt: Which is true about "uppers," pep pills and diet pills (stimulants) and driving?
choices: They safely replace sleep, so you can drive through the night
They may help briefly, but later can cause dizziness and poor focus
They speed up your reactions, which makes driving safer
They are only risky when taken together with alcohol
explanation: Stimulants can make a driver feel more alert for a short time. Later they can make you nervous and dizzy, hurt your concentration and affect your vision. They are not a substitute for rest.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AR p. 87, MT p. 83, NM p. 32, NH p. 15)

prompt: At a party you are handed a large specialty mixed drink. How much alcohol might it contain?
choices: Less than one standard drink, because of the mixers
Exactly one standard drink, like any other glass
About the same as a can of light beer
As much as several standard drinks
explanation: Specialty and mixed drinks often contain more than one shot of liquor, so one glass can equal several standard drinks. Mixers do not reduce the alcohol you take in.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AR p. 86, MT p. 81, NM p. 32)

prompt: How do impaired-driving laws treat drivers under 21 compared with adult drivers?
choices: They follow the same alcohol limit as adult drivers
They are held to a much lower alcohol limit than adults
They can only be charged if they cause a crash
Their limit applies only when they carry passengers
explanation: Every state has a "zero tolerance" law that makes it illegal for drivers under 21 to drive with even a small amount of alcohol, far below the adult limit. Check your state's exact limit in the State Cheat Sheet.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 57, AZ p. 59, GA p. 5, MT p. 82)
